## dns.axfr.allowed

**Nameserver allows zone transfers to anyone** · active · default severity **high**

A nameserver answers AXFR requests from arbitrary clients, handing out the whole zone: every host name, including internal and staging ones never meant to be discovered. Seta reads only the first message of the transfer and reports how many records it held.

**How to fix:** Restrict zone transfers to your secondary nameservers' addresses (BIND: allow-transfer; PowerDNS: allow-axfr-ips; NSD: provide-xfr), ideally with TSIG.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5936#section-6>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2015/04/13/dns-zone-transfer-axfr-requests-may-leak-domain-information>

## dns.caa.invalid

**CAA records block all issuance by mistake** · passive · default severity **medium**

The CAA records that apply to the domain contain a record CAs can't honor: an unknown property marked critical, or an issue value that isn't a CA domain name. CAs then refuse to issue (or renew) certificates, and the site breaks when the current certificate expires.

**How to fix:** Fix or remove the record: issue values are CA domain names such as "letsencrypt.org" or "pki.goog", and the critical flag (128) must only be set on tags CAs understand.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8659#section-4>

## dns.caa.missing

**No CAA records** · passive · default severity **low**

Neither the domain nor its parent domains publish CAA records, so any public CA may issue certificates for it. CAA limits issuance to the CAs you use, which blocks mis-issuance through other CAs' weaker validation.

**How to fix:** Publish CAA records naming the CAs you use, e.g. "example.com. CAA 0 issue \"letsencrypt.org\"", and optionally an iodef record for violation reports.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8659>

## dns.cname.dangling

**CNAME points at a name that doesn't exist** · passive · default severity **medium**

A CNAME's target doesn't exist (NXDOMAIN), so the name is broken. If the target's domain is unregistered or on a service that lets anyone create that name, it can be taken over.

**How to fix:** Remove the CNAME record, or point it at a name that exists. Check whether the target's domain has expired.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1034#section-3.6.2>

## dns.dnssec.invalid

**DNSSEC validation fails** · passive · default severity **critical**

The parent zone says the domain is signed (DS record), but the signatures don't validate: no key matches the DS, a signature doesn't verify, or signatures have expired. Validating resolvers (Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and many ISPs) then answer SERVFAIL, so the domain, its website and its mail are unreachable for a large share of users.

**How to fix:** Fix the chain at the DNS provider (re-enable signing, or finish the key rollover) and make the DS record at the registrar match the current key. If signing can't be fixed quickly, remove the DS record at the registrar to go back to an unsigned zone.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4035#section-5>
- <https://dnsviz.net/>

## dns.dnssec.missing

**Domain is not signed with DNSSEC** · passive · default severity **low**

The zone isn't protected by DNSSEC (no DS record at the parent), so resolvers can't detect forged answers from cache poisoning or on-path attackers. When the zone is signed but the parent has no DS record, the signatures are never checked.

**How to fix:** Enable DNSSEC signing at your DNS provider, then publish the DS record it gives you at your registrar. Most managed DNS providers do both in one click.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4033>
- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/dnssec-what-is-it-why-important-2019-03-05-en>

## dns.dnssec.weak_algorithm

**DNSSEC uses a deprecated algorithm** · passive · default severity **low**

The zone is signed with an algorithm RFC 8624 says must not or should not be used for signing (RSA/SHA-1, DSA, RSA/MD5, GOST), or the parent's DS uses a SHA-1 digest. Some validators already treat such zones as unsigned.

**How to fix:** Roll the zone over to ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 (algorithm 13) and publish a SHA-256 DS (digest type 2).

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8624#section-3.1>

## dns.nameserver.open_resolver

**Nameserver is an open resolver** · active · default severity **medium**

A nameserver answers recursive queries for names outside its zones from anyone. Open resolvers are used to amplify DDoS attacks and are easier targets for cache poisoning.

**How to fix:** Disable recursion on authoritative nameservers (BIND: recursion no; or allow-recursion limited to your own networks), and run recursive resolvers only for your own clients.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5358>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2013/03/29/dns-amplification-attacks>

## dns.takeover.possible

**Subdomain can be taken over** · passive · default severity **high**

A CNAME points at a cloud or SaaS resource (a storage bucket, an app, a Pages site) that no longer exists, on a service where anyone can create a resource with that name. Whoever claims it serves their content, cookies and phishing pages on your domain. Seta only looks for the service's "doesn't exist" signature and never tries to claim anything.

**How to fix:** Delete the CNAME record now, or recreate the resource it points at in your own account. Remove DNS records before deprovisioning the resources they point at.

**References:**

- <https://github.com/EdOverflow/can-i-take-over-xyz>
- <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subdomain_takeovers>
